title: Ohm's law
question: What is Ohm's law?

principle.name: Ohm's law
principle.formulaNote: voltage = current × resistance, so current = voltage ÷ resistance
principle.idea: Push harder and more current flows; make the path narrower and less flows. For a wire or resistor at a steady temperature, the current is exactly proportional to the voltage, and the number that links them is the resistance.

examples.title: The air fryer's heating element
examples.text: A 1,500 W element on 230 V must have R = 230² ÷ 1,500, about 35 Ω. The same current flows through the cord, but the element has about 500 times its resistance, so it takes almost all the heat.

examples.title: A washing machine's water heater
examples.text: A front loader's 2,000 W heater is about 26 Ω. At a sagging 200 V it gives only about three quarters of its heat, because P = V² ÷ R.

examples.title: Old fan regulators ran hot
examples.text: A resistive regulator slows a fan by adding a resistor in series. On low speed it can burn nearly as much power as the fan uses; capacitor and electronic regulators waste about a watt.

examples.title: Thick inverter battery cables
examples.text: 720 W from a 12 V battery needs about 60 A. Cable heat is I²R, so the cables must be as thick as a finger to stay cool and not waste volts.

examples.title: A car's starter motor
examples.text: Cranking an engine draws around 150 A from a 12 V battery. On a thin cable the voltage drop I × R alone could stop the engine turning over.

examples.title: A jammed mixer heats up fast
examples.text: A spinning motor makes a back voltage that holds its current down. Jam or overload the blades and only the winding's resistance is left to limit I = V ÷ R, so the current climbs, I²R heats the coils and the thermal overload protector trips.

examples.title: The TV's standby light
examples.text: A red LED on a 5 V rail needs a resistor of about (5 − 2) ÷ 0.02 = 150 Ω to set 20 mA. The backlight's driver chip measures its LED current as the voltage across a tiny resistor.

examples.title: Why MCBs trip
examples.text: A geyser, a heater and an iron on one circuit draw about 22 A. The heat in the wall wire climbs with the square of the current, so a 16 A MCB switches off to save the wire.

examples.title: Wet hands and RCCBs
examples.text: Dry skin can resist about 100,000 Ω, so 230 V drives a tingle of 2 mA. Wet skin can fall to about 1,000 Ω and the current to a deadly 150 mA, which is why RCCBs cut power at 30 mA.

hook: Twice the push, twice the flow: one line of algebra runs every heater, charger and fuse in your home. Drive electrons round a 3D circuit, see why they crawl while the light comes on instantly, and find where Ohm's law finally breaks.

explainer.title: Voltage pushes, resistance holds back
explainer.text: Current is how much charge flows each second. It equals the push, voltage, divided by the resistance: I = V ÷ R. Double the voltage and the current doubles; double the resistance and it halves. On a current–voltage graph that is a straight line.

explainer.title: Resistance turns electricity into heat
explainer.text: The heat made each second is P = I² × R, or V² ÷ R. A 1,500 W air fryer element is about 35 Ω. The cord carries the same current but has 500 times less resistance, so the element glows and the cord stays cool.

explainer.title: Low voltage needs fat cables
explainer.text: For the same power, a 12 V battery must push twenty times the current of a 230 V socket. Cable heat grows with current squared, so inverter and car starter cables are as thick as a finger.

explainer.title: MCBs guard wires, RCCBs guard you
explainer.text: Too many heaters on one circuit push the current past 16 A and an MCB trips to save the wire. Your body is a resistor too: wet skin lets 230 V drive a deadly current, so an RCCB cuts the power when 30 mA leaks away.

explainer.title: Where the straight line bends
explainer.text: A bulb filament's resistance rises about 14 times as it heats, so it surges at switch-on. LEDs barely conduct until about 2 V, then shoot up, so they need a resistor. And below 4.2 K mercury's resistance drops to exactly zero.

concepts.def: The electrical push that drives charge round a circuit, measured in volts (V).
How much electric charge flows past a point each second, measured in amps (A).
How strongly something opposes current, measured in ohms (Ω). One volt drives one amp through one ohm.
Energy per second, in watts: P = V × I = I² × R.
The slow average speed of electrons along a wire, well under a millimetre per second.
A material's own resistance for a 1 m cube; wire resistance is resistivity × length ÷ area.
Obeying Ohm's law: current in proportion to voltage, a straight I–V line.
A material whose resistance falls to exactly zero below a critical temperature.
